extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (novelists) looking to craft satisfying endings
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for writing the final chapter of a novel: promises to keep, ending types, structural beats, common mistakes, and a step-by-step framework to draft a satisfying close.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Character Arc Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: If your protagonist spent the entire novel learning something — to trust, to let go, to fight back, to forgive — then the ending must test that growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final challenge should be the one that can only be overcome by the person your protagonist has become, not the person they were at the start. If the ending's test doesn't connect to the character's growth, the arc feels decorative rather than structural. Examples: if your character learned courage, the climax must require courage; if they learned to sacrifice, the climax must demand sacrifice.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Plot Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: Every plot question you raised must be answered. Not all in the final chapter — but by the end of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you introduced a mystery, solve it. If you set up romantic tension, resolve it. If you planted a detail that seemed significant, make it pay off. Useful exercise: list every question your story raises (Who killed the victim? Will they get together? What's behind the locked door?). Make sure each one is either answered or deliberately left open in a way that feels intentional, not accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Genre Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres carry different ending expectations; know and honor the contract your genre creates with readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre expectations (examples): Romance — emotionally satisfying commitment between the leads (HEA or HFN); Mystery/Thriller — puzzle solved fairly; Fantasy/Sci‑Fi — world-level stakes addressed; Literary — emotional understanding and earned ambiguity. Break this at your own risk; understand what readers expect and meet those core expectations even when playing with form.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Thematic Promise
rubrics_metrics.description: The story has been asking a question all along — about love, justice, identity, power, grief, forgiveness — and the ending needs to arrive at that question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ending doesn't need to answer the theme definitively but should arrive at it. The character's final action should embody the theme through demonstration, not through expository dialogue. The ending should feel like the events were in service of something larger than plot mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 1: The Resolved Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: All major threads are tied up. The protagonist achieves (or definitively fails to achieve) their goal. The reader closes the book with a sense of completion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for standalone novels and genre fiction where readers expect closure (romance, mystery, thriller). Risk: If resolution is too complete, it can feel sanitized. Fix: resolve major threads but leave one small, human-scaled question open (emotional rather than plot) so the ending breathes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 2: The Bittersweet Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist achieves their goal — but at a cost. Or they lose what they wanted and gain what they needed. Victory and loss coexist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for stories about sacrifice, coming-of-age, or themes where meaningful things come with a price. Why it works: mirrors life honestly and honors complexity, eliciting both sadness and satisfaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 3: The Twist Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A final revelation recontextualizes everything the reader thought they knew (unreliable narrator revealed, ally is villain, protagonist was dead all along, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for psychological thrillers, mysteries, and stories about perception vs. reality. Rule: the twist must be surprising but inevitable — readers should be able to reread and find planted seeds. If the twist can't be traced backward, it's a trick, not a twist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 4: The Circular Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The story ends where it began — but the protagonist (and the reader) understand the starting point differently now; setting may be the same, emotional landscape transformed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for character-driven narratives, coming-of-age stories, and stories about cycles. Why it works: creates a musical sense of completeness and demonstrates transformation through contrast between beginning and end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 5: The Ambiguous Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: The story ends without definitive resolution; questions remain and the reader is left to interpret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for literary fiction and stories emphasizing complexity or the journey over the destination. Test: does the ambiguity add to the reader's experience or subtract from it? If readers feel enriched by filling the gap, you've succeeded; if they feel frustrated, you've likely withheld too much. Choose ambiguity with conviction — know what you think happened and leave space deliberately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type 6: The Pyrrhic Victory
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist wins — but the cost is so devastating that the victory feels hollow; victory comes with devastating loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best for epic narratives, war stories, and stories about power, corruption, or moral compromise. Use when you want to ask whether the goal was worth pursuing in the first place: the war is won but the country is destroyed; the killer is caught but the detective has lost what made them human.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 1: The Climax (85–90% of the novel)
rubrics_metrics.description: The final confrontation — where everything has been building toward; the protagonist faces their greatest challenge; stakes at their highest; outcome uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The climax should be where plot and character arc collide. The external challenge should demand the internal growth the protagonist has undergone. One critical principle: the protagonist must be active in the climax — they must make a choice or take action. If someone else saves them or the resolution comes by coincidence, the climax collapses and the ending feels unearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 2: The Resolution (90–95%)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the climax's intensity, the resolution shows consequences — what changed, who survived, what was lost and gained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is where plot threads are tied up and emotional payoff happens. Give the resolution space to let readers feel the weight of events; avoid trying to resolve everything in a couple of pages. Common mistake: rushing the resolution; fix by budgeting the final 10–15% of the novel and giving decompression time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beat 3: The Final Image (95–100%)
rubrics_metrics.description: The very last scene — the final moment the reader experiences before closing the book; the aftertaste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final images typically do one of three things: mirror the opening (same place, transformed meaning), point forward (a small glimpse of what's next), or crystallize the theme (a single image, action, or line that distills the story's emotional truth). Write the final image to leave a lasting impression — it should be the concentrated distillation of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake 1: The Deus Ex Machina
rubrics_metrics.description: A character or force that was never set up suddenly appears and solves the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Why it's bad: destroys reader trust and makes the protagonist's struggle meaningless. Fix: ensure the ending emerges from the protagonist's decisions and the world you've established; if resolution requires something new, plant it earlier (even subtly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake 2: The Rushed Resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax is intense and well-executed, but the aftermath gets two paragraphs and a time skip; relationships built over hundreds of pages are resolved in a sentence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix: budget your final 10–15% carefully. Give the resolution room so readers can decompress and feel the emotional payoff; don't try to answer five major questions in a paragraph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake 3: The Theme Speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A character delivers a monologue that explains the theme of the story directly (e.g., 'I guess what I learned is that family is what matters most').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have to tell the reader your theme, you haven't shown it. The theme should be embedded in action during the climax and resolution, not stated in dialogue after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake 4: The Unearned Happy Ending
rubrics_metrics.description: Everything works out perfectly with no plausible cost: every relationship repaired, every wound healed, every character gets exactly what they wanted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers reject implausible happy endings. Fix: let something be lost even in a happy ending. The best happy endings contain a grain of cost that honors the journey's complexity and makes the ending feel real.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistake 5: The False Ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer doesn't commit to an ending — not because ambiguity serves the story, but because they couldn't decide; the result feels evasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fix: choose ambiguity with conviction. Know what you think happened and then leave enough space for the reader to wonder, not so much that they feel abandoned. Deliberate ambiguity should enrich the experience, not replace clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1: List your promises
rubrics_metrics.description: Write down every major question your story raises, every character arc it tracks, every thematic thread it follows. This is your fulfillment checklist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist to audit the ending: every promise should be answered or deliberately left open. This step operationalizes the 'Character Arc', 'Plot', 'Genre', and 'Thematic' promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2: Choose your ending type
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on your story's genre, tone, and theme, decide which of the six ending types best serves your narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You don't have to commit permanently, but having a direction sharpens drafting. Match ending type to genre contract and thematic needs (e.g., don't give a romance an unresolved anti‑HEA unless you subvert the genre knowingly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 3: Write the climax first
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft the climax to ensure it tests your protagonist's growth and that the protagonist is active in resolving the core conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make sure stakes justify the book's buildup and that the climax forces the internal change to manifest through action. Writing the climax first helps ensure the ending is earned and structurally coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 4: Write the resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Address each promise on your checklist, weaving resolutions into scenes that feel natural and emotionally resonant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't resolve mechanically; give each thread space and emotional weight. The resolution should show consequences and let readers feel the aftermath rather than rush to closure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 5: Write the final image last
rubrics_metrics.description: After you know how everything resolves, find the single image, line, or moment that distills the emotional truth of your story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final image is the reader's last impression — make it count. It should crystallize theme, mirror the opening, or point forward subtly. Compose it after resolution so it accurately reflects what the story has become.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 6: Audit against your opening
rubrics_metrics.description: Read your first chapter and your last chapter back-to-back to check coherence and whether the ending delivers on the opening's promise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the opening and ending feel disconnected, something in the arc has drifted. Use this audit to spot missed promises, tonal mismatches, or character inconsistencies and revise accordingly.
